scope_note: Full-source boundary-date probe covering 9 targets and 8 contexts. Complete retained bodies, XML date bounds, excluded layers, apparatus and source voices were read; all records remain candidate evidence only.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s two-block note to Sharpey finishes an administrative exchange about a candidate: Hooker will enquire whether the person can attend once proposed, but hesitates without knowing that the candidate is on the list. Darwin is writing hurriedly to catch the post.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [1853–72?]; XML bounds 1853-01-01 to 1872-12-31. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing fragment/short note; the candidate and Hooker are reported, not voices of the body.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The preceding candidate discussion is not preserved and no scientific prompt is identified.

evidence.quote: When proposed Hooker will enquire if he can attend

record_reviews.summary: Spruce answers an earlier request about plants and ant-inhabited leaf structures. He cannot revisit the locality because of health and travel limits, sends a newly rewritten memoir on insect-produced plant modifications for Darwin to assess and pass to the Linnean Society, admits the ant evidence is incomplete, and reflects on how Origin shaped his own botanical thinking. Several passages are excised or damaged, including the opening.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 1 Apr 1869]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1869-03-31. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Incoming Spruce voice; his memoir, missing ants and retrospective reading of Darwin remain separate layers.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s original questions and the full missing portions are unavailable; the memoir transfer is prospective and not a demonstrated Darwin response.

evidence.quote: send it to you by this day’s post
no definite account of the ants infesting the plants

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Stokes a single coral-reef geology question: whether coral masses or shell beds lie yards above high-water mark on the coast facing the barrier reef.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [after 31 May 1837]; XML bounds 1837-06-01 to 1882-12-31. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Stokes’s answer is not preserved and the broad post-1837 date does not establish a period pair.

evidence.quote: masses of coral or beds of shells some yards above high water mark

record_reviews.summary: Swinhoe reports Chinese claims about Mallard–Muscovy hybrids, a detailed dog-morality story attributed to Consul colleague T. Watters, a retracted observation of thrush spurs, and his cautious inference about wild Bos and domestic cattle in Formosa and southern China. His own corrections and qualifications matter: he says the spur observation was mistaken and will not identify the wild cattle stocks without more evidence.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 1 Oct 1865?]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1865-09-30. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Incoming Swinhoe voice; Watters’s dog story and Chinese accounts are explicitly third-party testimony.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s antecedent questions are not preserved; this mixed report cannot be matched to a particular Darwin response.

evidence.quote: The story that I am about to relate has been told to me by Mr. T. Watters
I now think that I must have been mistaken

record_reviews.summary: Tearle proposes a theological reconciliation between Genesis and Darwinian evolution, beginning with man as a superior animal later marked as God’s image. He presents the idea as his own tentative theory and asks Darwin to judge its novelty and tenability; the retained body has a damaged/unfinished middle and formal closing.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 16] Apr 1880; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1880-04-15. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Incoming Tearle letter; biblical quotation and speculative argument belong to Tearle.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No Darwin reply or identifiable prior prompt survives; this unsolicited theory is not a demonstrated exchange.

evidence.quote: some solution to the two first chapters of Genesis
Whether my theory has been made before

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Blair, who had previously advised Darwin’s son about blushing in blind people, for observations on expression in people born blind. He sends a worldwide questionnaire, asks specifically about astonishment, shoulder shrugging and children’s sulking, and requests permission to quote Blair’s observations on Blair’s authority.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 16 Mar 1871]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1871-03-15. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing request; the son’s earlier visit and the proposed asylum contact are reported context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Blair’s answer is absent; the request is an initiated enquiry rather than a response.

evidence.quote: The enclosed query has been sent all over the world
persons born blind

record_reviews.summary: Darwin tests Tollet’s report that cobwebs disappeared from a hedge. He marks thirteen webs, revisits them with Emma as witness, finds marked webs unchanged while close inspection reveals many other webs, and contrasts his own audacious conclusion with Emma’s charitable alternative that Tollet’s sharp sight might explain the discrepancy.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 1 Oct 1846; XML bounds 1846-10-01 to 1871-10-01. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored observational reply; Emma is a named witness to the inspection, not co-author.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Tollet’s earlier report is not present; the wide 1846–1871 date range prevents treating this as a secure period exchange.

evidence.quote: I marked 13 with red worsted
Emma, who has so good a heart

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks St Barbe to obtain careful broker information for about £17,000 of railway shares, preferring guaranteed or preference shares that participate after ordinary shares rise. He names Lancaster and Carlisle, Newcastle and Carlisle, Great Northern of Scotland and North Staffordshire possibilities, and asks about a reported canal guarantee whose scale he cannot verify.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 3 July 1862]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1862-07-02. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored financial inquiry; broker and reported railway terms are external information.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: St Barbe’s reply and broker evidence are absent; no scientific or period relationship is proposed.

evidence.quote: I wish to invest through the Union Bank about £17,000 in Railway Shares

record_reviews.summary: Walsh forwards a one-block extract from Hartman’s 1851 journal about the periodical cicada in Pennsylvania. Only the beginning of the extract survives in this record, ending mid-sentence (“drums”), so the source extent is explicitly incomplete and no Darwin-authored framing is present.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [before 31 Oct 1868]; XML bounds 1809-01-01 to 1868-10-30. This boundary record is not period-selection eligible.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Incoming extract/memorandum with Hartman as the quoted journal author and Walsh as sender.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Darwin’s prompt and the rest of Hartman’s account are missing; no response endpoint is identified.

evidence.quote: Extracts from a Journal of the doings of Cic. septemdecim

record_reviews.summary: Darwin tells Stokes that copied letters unexpectedly returned to him and that a note bearing Darwin’s signature had apparently been sent to Governor Grey inside Stokes’s proof-sheets. He asks how this happened, worries about appearing impertinent, and offers to explain to Grey.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 3 Nov 1846; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; copied documents and Governor Grey are reported context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Stokes’s preceding correspondence is referenced but no new scientific input is involved.

evidence.quote: It places me in the position of wishing to make myself presumptuously impertinent to him

record_reviews.summary: Stokes replies that Darwin’s 3 November letter and enclosure surprised and annoyed him. He remembers receiving the note but thought he destroyed it, regrets that it reached Governor Grey, and promises to find the “mischief maker.”
record_reviews.date_assessment: 6 Nov 1846; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Incoming Stokes reply; the disputed note’s route is the subject, not a scientific source.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: This answers 1017’s document-routing problem, but both records are 1846 context and outside the nominal boundary probe.

evidence.quote: It gives me great concern to think, that I should in any way be the means

record_reviews.summary: Darwin resolves the Stokes/Grey issue by saying he enclosed the proper note to Grey and believes the mistaken note travelled in Stokes’s proof-sheet to the printers. He returns a South Australian letter, congratulates Stokes on his book and the Duke’s recognition, and closes warmly.
record_reviews.date_assessment: [c. 26 Nov 1846]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing continuation of the document-routing correspondence; the returned South Australian letter is a separate enclosed source.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No new prompt is preserved beyond Stokes’s 1019 reply; the date is approximate and outside the target period.

evidence.quote: my note went in your proof-sheet to the Printers

record_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges Stokes’s books, invites him to Down for a weekend with mutual scientific friends, gives train and carriage directions, and expects Hooker and Waterhouse. This is a social invitation and logistics note, not a scientific reply.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 2 Jan [1847]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; named scientists are prospective guests.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Stokes’s response is absent and the 1847 date is outside this boundary packet.

evidence.quote: will you give us the pleasure of joining them

record_reviews.summary: Darwin tells Sharpey he cannot offer special research suggestions for the expedition because he has not attended to the region, but recommends collecting Carboniferous plants and investigating glacial action and erratic boulders. He says the Admiralty Manual already covers general suggestions and closes with an explicit inability to add more.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 24 Jan [1857]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing advisory letter; expedition and Admiralty Manual are institutional contexts.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Sharpey’s request is not preserved as an endpoint here; this is a bounded answer to a missing administrative prompt.

evidence.quote: I really am quite unable to offer any special points of research

record_reviews.summary: Darwin comments on library catalogues, supports acquiring Agassiz, weighs Low’s domestic animals and Macgillivray’s birds, recommends Davidson, Sorby, Beckles and Andrew Smith for candidates, and forwards General Sabine’s grant-committee letter while declining to attend. The F-marked source is a complete five-block letter, not a fragment.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 9 Apr [1857]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Sabine’s letter is a forwarded third-party document and candidate assessments are Darwin’s.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Sharpey’s catalogue and committee prompt are referenced but not separately preserved; no new direct pair is established.

evidence.quote: General Sabine in letter to Sir C. Lyell, forwarded to me

record_reviews.summary: Darwin strongly supports Hancock for a Royal Medal, suggests Prestwich for geology, and uses the occasion to urge Sharpey to remember Lyell for the Copley Medal. He explains his counterfactual test of merit—what science would be without the person—and cites Forbes as an example of Lyell’s influence.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 22 May [1857]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing advocacy; Huxley’s view and Sharpey’s information are reported, while the medal judgments are Darwin’s.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Sharpey’s preceding question is not preserved; this is a recommendation rather than a reply to a source-complete incoming letter.

evidence.quote: the future Historian of the Natural Sciences, will rank Lyell’s labours

record_reviews.summary: Darwin revises his medal advice after hearing from Hooker that Lindley has been proposed for the Royal Medal. He explains why his botanical reading qualifies his opinion, says Lindley should outrank Hancock or Prestwich for this medal, then worries that his earlier private letter was read to the Royal Society Council and may have sounded dogmatic.
record_reviews.date_assessment: 2 June [1857]; XML date is within period.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin-authored outgoing; Hooker’s report and the Council reading are reported institutional context.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The earlier Sharpey prompt and Hooker’s communication are not preserved as separate endpoint bodies; no new relationship is asserted.

evidence.quote: my letter to you was read to the Council
